summary.text: An 18-year old first gravida at 31 weeks of gestation developed severe sepsis from an obstructive pyelonephritis and was referred with progressive hypoxic lung failure and need for intubation. She was transferred to an ICU and received lung protective ventilation, corticosteroid prophylaxis and magnesium sulfate. Fetal monitoring was normal, with a eutrophic male fetus, normal amniotic fluid and no fetal morphological abnormalities.

During ICU treatment she received remifentanil, fentanyl, nalbuphine, propofol and midazolam. Two days after opioid introduction an enlarged fetal bladder was seen, and four days after induction ultrasound showed a decompressed bladder with thickened wall, hematoma and significant ascites; a possible spontaneous bladder rupture with urinary ascites was suspected and an expectant approach with daily monitoring was chosen.

Fetal ascites kept increasing and amniotic fluid decreased; nine days after the suspected rupture doppler velocimetry showed progressive deterioration, anhydramnios was detected and an abdominal compartment syndrome was imminent. Preterm caesarean delivery was decided on and performed; the placenta detached immediately after delivery.

The child did not adapt, with APGAR 1/5/7, and ventilation and circulation were established only after percutaneous drainage of 350 mL of abdominal fluid, which was confirmed to be urine; ultrasound confirmed a dorsolateral bladder defect. Non-operative management failed with rising ascites and high creatinine, and the bladder was closed surgically on the fifth day of life. The neonate recovered well, posterior urethral valves were ruled out and regular voiding followed catheter removal.
